_about: Reusable domain knowledge for character rigging and animation in Maya and Blender, researched 2026-10-16. Every statement carries a trust tier and a source id. Tiers: official = the application vendor's own documentation; community = forum or Q&A advice (practical, not guaranteed, often for older versions); tutorial = what a tutorial narrator said or showed (menu names as spoken); author = the assistant's reading, NOT verified. Statements are paraphrased, not copied. NOT covered: Houdini animation, retargeting, Motion Clips and mocap (Houdini has eight entries: skeleton, orient, mirror, IK Chains, Rig Doctor, capture weights, AutoRig, KineFX workflow), Reddit threads and Blender Stack Exchange (the search tool never returned them), anything checked inside a running Maya or Blender. Menu names differ between versions: Autodesk pages cited here are for Maya 2009 to 2026 as stated per source, the Blender manual is the 'latest' manual of 2026-10-16.

phrases: make the joints face the right way
my joints twist the wrong way
joint axes point in different directions
bones rotate on the wrong axis

ui.note: The Autodesk page lists the options but gives no menu path; the path 'Skeleton > Orient Joint' is as spoken in tutorials.

prerequisites: The joint chain exists and is parented root to tip.
Select the root joint of the chain first, and turn on 'Orient children of selected joints' if the whole chain should change.

facts.text: The Primary Axis is the local axis that points down the bone toward its child.
A joint cannot rotate around its Primary Axis: with Primary Axis X, the local X axis will not rotate.
Primary and Secondary Axis cannot be the same axis; if you choose one already in use, Maya switches the other.
Setting Secondary Axis to None lets Maya choose it automatically.
'Orient children of selected joints' makes the settings apply to every joint below the selected one; with it off only the selected joint changes.

verify.text: Turn on 'Toggle Local Axes Visibility' (or display local rotation axes) and look down the chain: every joint's primary axis should point at its child and the secondary axes should line up.

mistakes.text: Letting Maya orient automatically on a curved chain can flip axes, because it does not know which way is 'up' for the joints; choose a Secondary Axis World Orientation to fix the up direction.
Orienting the joints after skinning moves the rest pose of the skeleton; orient before binding.

symptom_phrases: joint won't rotate on one axis
can't rotate joint around x
joint locked on one rotation axis
troubleshooting.cause: That axis was chosen as the Primary Axis, and a joint does not rotate around its primary axis.
fix: Check which axis is the Primary Axis in Orient Joint Options.
Rotate around one of the other two axes, or re-orient with a different Primary Axis.

phrases: make the leg follow the foot
move the foot and the leg bends
pin the foot to the ground while the hip moves

ui.note: Options named on the Autodesk IK Handle Tool page (2009-2011). The two usual solvers are ikRPsolver (rotate plane) and ikSCsolver (single chain).

prerequisites: A joint chain with a slight bend at the knee or elbow, oriented consistently.
Know the start joint (hip) and the end joint (ankle) of the limb.

outline.text: Choose the IK Handle tool (Skeleton > Create IK Handle).
Click the start joint (for a leg, the hip), then the end joint (the ankle); the handle appears at the end joint.
Move the handle to check that the limb bends to follow it.

facts.text: 'Solver Enable' is on by default, so the handle works immediately.
'Autopriority' (off by default) sets the handle's priority from its start joint's depth in the hierarchy.
'Sticky' (off by default) holds the handle in place while other joints or handles are posed.

verify.text: Move the IK handle: the whole limb should bend to follow it and the end joint should stay on the handle.

mistakes.text: Building the limb as a perfectly straight chain makes the IK solver pick the bend direction unpredictably, so the knee or elbow can flip.

symptom_phrases: knee flips
elbow bends the wrong way
arm bending wrong way
leg bends backwards when I move the ik handle
knee goes wonky
knee popping
knee pops the wrong way
knee snaps backwards
troubleshooting.cause: The joint chain had no bend (or the wrong bend) when the IK handle was created, so Maya has no preferred bend direction; a missing or badly placed pole vector can also flip it.
fix: Disable the IK handle, rotate the knee or elbow slightly in the direction it should bend, set the preferred angle, then enable the handle again.
If it still flips, add a pole vector control in front of the knee (see the pole vector entry).
As a last resort rebuild the chain drawn from the front view with a slight bend.

phrases: make the knee bend the right direction
tell the ik which way to bend
stop the knee from popping the wrong way
keep the knee from snapping backwards

outline.text: Select the top joint of the chain (the hip), then use Skeleton > Set Preferred Angle so Maya knows which way the knee should bend, before creating the IK handle.
If the handle already exists: disable it, pre-bend the joint, assume/set the preferred angle, then enable it again.

mistakes.text: A chain with no initial bend gives the solver no hint, which is the usual cause of a flipped knee.

phrases: control which way the knee points
make the knee follow a control

outline.text: Create a control (a locator or curve) and place it in front of the knee, not too close to it.
Select the control and the IK handle, then Constrain > Pole Vector.

conflicts.text: Sources disagree on the selection order: the UCLA notes say select the control (locator) first and the IK handle second; a Polycount reply says the IK handle first, then the control. Check which order works in your Maya version and tell the learner to test it.

verify.text: Move the pole vector control around the knee: the knee should turn toward it without the leg flipping.

mistakes.text: Putting the pole vector control behind the knee, or on the limb's own axis, can make the leg flip.

phrases: attach the controller to the joint
make the joint follow the control

facts.text: 'Maintain Offset' keeps the object's existing position and rotation relative to its target when the constraint is made.
'Weight' only matters when there is more than one target.
'Constraint Axes' can limit the constraint to X, Y or Z instead of All.

The Autodesk page does not state the selection order. In tutorials the target(s) are selected first and the object to be constrained last (select the IK joint, then the FK joint, then the skin joint).

verify.text: Move or rotate the driver (the target): the constrained object should follow. With two targets, change the Weight values and check it moves between them.

mistakes.text: Forgetting Maintain Offset makes the constrained object jump to the target when the constraint is created.

phrases: switch between two ways of controlling a leg
let the animator choose ik or fk
one control to change between two rigs

outline.text: Build three joint chains: the skin (bind) chain, an IK chain and an FK chain (duplicate the skin chain twice and rename the copies, for example with Modify > Search and Replace Names).
Parent-constrain each skin joint to its IK joint and its FK joint (target joints first, skin joint last), with Maintain Offset on.
Create a switch control and add a float attribute (for example FK_IK_Switch) with a minimum of 0 and a maximum of 1.

Connect the attribute to the two constraint weights so one rises as the other falls; the video routes one weight through a reverse node for the opposite value. A Set Driven Key on the weights is the other common method.
Test by changing the switch from 0 to 1 and checking the skin joints follow the FK chain, then the IK chain.

verify.text: Set the switch to 0 and to 1 and move the IK and FK controls separately: the skin joints should follow only the chain the switch selects, and nothing should jump when you change it.

mistakes.text: Switching modes mid-animation makes the limb jump back to where the other chain's pose was, unless the FK controls are first matched to the IK pose (or the reverse).

phrases: reset the position values to zero
clean up the transforms before rigging
delete the history and freeze the transformations

facts.text: Freezing does not change joint translation, because joint translation defines the bone length.
Older Autodesk help advises freezing (and deleting history) before operations such as stitch, align, attach, sculpt, wire and wrinkle.

prerequisites: Do it on the mesh and on controls before binding or constraining.

mistakes.text: Skipping 'delete history' and 'freeze transformations' on the mesh before binding is one of the most common causes of a bind that misbehaves.

phrases: make the mesh follow the skeleton
attach the mesh to the joints
bind the character to the rig
my mesh doesn't move with the joints

ui.path: Skin > Bind Skin > Smooth Bind (options box)

prerequisites: Delete history and freeze transformations on the mesh first.
The skeleton is oriented and in a clean rest pose (T-pose or A-pose).
Select the skeleton's root joint and the mesh.

facts.text: The hierarchy-based bind method is the default and is meant for characters: it stops a joint on one side from influencing the other side's skin.
The Heat Map method treats each joint as a heat source inside the mesh; it only works on polygon meshes.
Max influences is how many joints may affect each skin point (default 5 in the help).

verify.text: Rotate a joint: the mesh around it should follow. Undo afterwards.

mistakes.text: Do not use Delete by Type > History on a bound mesh: it can remove the skin cluster, leaving the skeleton moving but the mesh stuck. Use Delete by Type > Non-Deformer History on a bound mesh instead.
Binding a mesh that was not frozen and cleaned first causes odd results such as the mesh merging toward the first joint.

symptom_phrases: mesh doesn't move with the skeleton
mesh stays still when the joints move
mesh is no longer moving with skeleton
skeleton moves but the mesh doesn't
joints move but mesh stays
troubleshooting.cause: The skin binding is missing or was removed: often history was deleted after binding, or the bind was never made on this mesh.
fix: Select the mesh and look in the Channel Box or Node Editor for a skinCluster; if there is none, the bind is gone.
Rebind with Skin > Bind Skin > Smooth Bind (after freezing and deleting history on the mesh), or restore from a saved scene.
In future use Delete by Type > Non-Deformer History after binding.

phrases: fix the way the mesh bends
the elbow collapses when it bends
open the paint skin weights options
paint white where you want more influence

facts.text: 'Normalize Weights' is a separate setting from the paint operation: in Interactive mode (the default) the weights on all influences are kept adding up to 1.0.
Turning normalization off allows weights above or below one in total and can produce odd deformation.
Weight Hammer repairs selected vertices whose weights cause bad deformation; Move Weights takes weight from a source influence and gives it to target influences.

verify.text: Pose the joint through its range and look at the area you painted; it should bend smoothly with no pinching or sticking to the wrong bone.

phrases: add a slider to a controller
add a channel to the control
add an extra setting to the rig control

ui.path: Edit > Add Attribute (Channel Box) / Modify > Add Attribute (older help)
ui.note: Autodesk's 2013 help puts the command in the Modify menu; tutorials show it under the Channel Box Edit menu. Look for it in both.

conflicts.text: The menu location differs between sources (Modify > Add Attribute in the 2013 help, Edit > Add Attribute in the tutorials). Tell the learner to look in both.

facts.text: 'Minimum' and 'Maximum' limit the values that can be entered for a numeric attribute.
'Keyable' makes the attribute keyable; 'Displayable' shows it in the Channel Box without being keyable; 'Hidden' hides it.

verify.text: Select the control: the new attribute should appear in the Channel Box with the range you set.

phrases: drive a setting from a slider
connect a slider to the rig

ui.path: Animate > Set Driven Key > Set (the Set Driven Key window)
ui.note: The window and its buttons are on the Autodesk page; the menu that opens it is not stated there.

outline.text: Select the driver (for example the switch control) and click Load Driver; select the driven object and click Load Driven.
Set the driver attribute and the driven attribute to the first state and press Key; change both to the second state and press Key again.

phrases: make the mesh follow the bones
attach my character to the armature
parent the mesh to the rig
bind the mesh to the skeleton

ui.path: Object > Parent > Armature Deform (Ctrl-P, 'Set Parent To')

prerequisites: The armature's bones that should move the mesh are set to Deform (Properties > Bone > Deform).
Mesh in a clean rest pose; apply scale on both the mesh and the armature (see mistakes).

outline.text: Select the mesh (the child) first, then select the armature last so it is the active object.
Press Ctrl-P and choose 'With Automatic Weights' in the 'Set Parent To' menu.

facts.text: 'With Empty Groups' creates empty vertex groups named after each deforming bone; 'With Automatic Weights' also fills them using a 'bone heat' distance method.
Automatic weights can leave parts of the mesh not deforming as expected on complex armatures; the manual says you then adjust the weights by hand.

verify.text: Go into Pose Mode, rotate a bone, and check the mesh around it follows; undo the pose afterwards.

mistakes.text: Selecting the armature before the mesh (wrong order) parents the wrong way round.

symptom_phrases: bone heat weighting failed
automatic weights failed
failed to find solution for one or more bones
bone heat weighting: failed to find solution
automatic weights not working
troubleshooting.cause: The automatic weighting could not compute weights for some bones; reports point to the mesh itself (loose or non-manifold geometry, duplicate vertices, bad scale) and not the rig.
fix: Clean the mesh: Mesh > Clean Up > Merge by Distance, Delete Loose, and look for non-manifold geometry (Select > Select All by Trait > Non Manifold).
Apply scale on the mesh and the armature (Object > Apply > Scale).
Check that no deforming bone is too small or sits outside the mesh.
If it still fails, use With Empty Groups and paint the weights by hand.

phrases: make the leg follow the foot
move the foot and the leg bends

ui.path: Pose Mode > Bone Constraint properties > Add Bone Constraint > Inverse Kinematics (or Shift-I)

outline.text: Make a target bone (the foot control) and, for the bend direction, a pole target bone (the knee control) in front of the knee.

In Pose Mode, select the last bone of the limb (the shin) and add an Inverse Kinematics constraint; set Target (and Pole Target) and set Chain Length to the number of bones that should move (2 for thigh and shin).

facts.text: Chain Length is the number of bones affected, counting from the constrained bone up through its parents; 1 affects only that bone, 2 the bone and its parent, 0 means all ancestors up to the root.
The Pole Target decides the roll of the chain, which for a limb means the direction the knee or elbow points.
The IK constraint can work without a Target: the chain tip can then be moved freely and only its ancestors are constrained.
'Use Tail' makes the end of the chain the bone's tail; unticking it uses the bone's head.

verify.text: Move the target bone: the thigh and shin should rotate so the foot follows. Move the pole target: the knee should turn toward it without flipping.

mistakes.text: Bones with no initial bend give the solver no direction, so the knee can bend backwards; give the leg a slight bend in Edit Mode with the knee pushed forward.
A pole target placed behind the knee or very close to it can make the leg flip; put it in front of the knee and a little way out.

symptom_phrases: knee bends the wrong way in blender
knee flips when I move the foot
knee pointing sideways
character doesn't follow knee pole correctly
knee going wonky
ik always at 90 degrees
troubleshooting.cause: No initial bend on the chain, a pole target in the wrong place, or the Pole Angle not matching the bone's roll.
fix: In Edit Mode move the knee joint slightly forward so the chain is bent the right way.
Put the pole target bone in front of the knee, a little away from the mesh.
Adjust the constraint's Pole Angle in Pose Mode until the knee points at the pole target.
If it bends on several axes, lock the IK rotation on the shin so it bends on one axis only (the lock must be on the shin, the bone in the chain).

phrases: bones rotate on the wrong axis

ui.path: Edit Mode > Armature > Bone Roll > Recalculate Roll (Shift-N)

facts.text: Bone roll is the bone's default rotation around its own length, part of its rest pose, and is edited in Edit Mode.
Recalculate Roll aligns the roll of the selected bones to a reference: a local tangent, a global axis, the active bone, the view axis or the 3D cursor.

verify.text: Show the bones' axes (Properties > Armature > Viewport Display > Axes) and check each bone's Z axis points the way you chose.

phrases: copy the left side bones to the right
prerequisites: Name the bones with a left/right convention (for example .L and .R, or Left/Right) so Blender can pair them.

facts.text: Symmetrize mirrors the selected bones along the X axis using the bone naming convention.
Bones whose names do not show a side are ignored; existing opposite-side bones are overwritten.
Bones can be renamed in the Bone properties Name field or by double-clicking them in the Outliner.

verify.text: Check the other side now has bones with the side swapped in their names, positioned as a mirror image.

phrases: make the bones for the leg
place the joints on the character
put the joints where the knee bends
adjust the position of the joints

outline.text: Go to the front or side view and use the joint tool to click the joints in order from the top of the limb down (for a leg: hip, knee, ankle, ball, toe).
Adjust each joint so it sits where the real body bends (hip, knee, ankle), checking in more than one view.
Give the knee or elbow a slight bend in the direction it should fold, so IK later knows which way to bend.

verify.text: In the Outliner or hierarchy the joints form one chain, each parented to the one before it, and from the front and side views each joint sits at a bend point inside the mesh.

mistakes.text: A perfectly straight limb chain makes later IK unpredictable (the knee can flip).

phrases: add a side to the joint names

outline.text: Rename every joint so the name says its side, its body part and what kind of joint it is (the video used names such as left_hip_skin_JNT, left_knee_skin_JNT); unique names are needed for later tools such as search-and-replace renaming and mirroring.

verify.text: In the Outliner every joint has a unique name that starts or ends with its side.

phrases: make a control for the foot
make controls for the ik and fk
make a controller for each joint
create controllers for the ik and fk chains

ui.path: Create > NURBS Primitives > Circle (a common control shape)
ui.note: Tutorials use curve shapes such as circles, or a controller-creation tool or script; the exact tool varies.

outline.text: Make a curve shape (often a circle) for each joint you want the animator to grab, size and turn it to suit the joint, and name it after the joint it will drive.
Place each control at its joint, delete its history and freeze its transformations so its channels read zero, then parent or constrain it so it drives the joint.

verify.text: Each control is visible, selectable, named after its joint, and moving or rotating it moves or rotates the joint it drives.

phrases: make the joint copy the rotation of the control

ui.path: Constrain > Orient / Point / Scale (shown in tutorials as separate menu items)

outline.text: Select the target (for example the FK control) first and the object it should drive (the FK joint) last, then choose the constraint type; use an orient constraint to pass on rotation only.

facts.text: The Parent Constraint page documents Maintain Offset, Constraint Axes and Weight; the same ideas are used in tutorials for orient and point constraints, but this page does not describe those other constraint types.

verify.text: Rotate the target: only the constrained property (rotation, for an orient constraint) should follow on the driven object.

phrases: put the control in a group
create separate groups for ik and fk controllers
place the ik handle under the controller

outline.text: Put each control in its own group (an offset group) so the control itself reads zero while the group holds its position.
Keep the IK controls and the FK controls in separate groups so each set can be shown, hidden or moved as one.
Place the IK handle under its IK controller so moving the controller moves the handle.

facts.text: Freeze Transformations resets translate/rotate/scale values to zero without moving the object, which is how a control is made to read zero in its place.

verify.text: Select the control: its translate and rotate channels read 0 and scale 1 while it still sits at the joint.

phrases: place the joints and maya creates the rig

ui.path: Skeleton > Quick Rig (as described in the tutorial; the exact path varies by Maya version)

outline.text: In the beginner tutorial you mark where the wrist, elbow and other joints belong on the character and Maya then creates the rig for you, after which you bind the mesh and test by moving joints.

mistakes.text: An automatic rig gives few manual steps to learn from; it is a different lesson from building a rig by hand.

phrases: build a rig automatically in houdini
add ik to the legs and arms
add fk controls to the skeleton

ui.options_in: component menu filled from the installed rig components, not a fixed parameter list

prerequisites: A skeleton and the skin shape exist and are packed into one character with APEX Pack Character (defaults: Shape Path /Base.shp, Skeleton Path /Base.skel).
The skeleton points carry the tags the components look for (the docs add them with Attribute Adjust Tags); components select joints by tag.

outline.text: Pack the shape and skeleton with APEX Pack Character and check the result in the rig tree view.
Add an APEX AutoRig Component with Component Source FK Transform, then one with Bone Deform.
Add controls and the spine, then Multi IK for arms and legs, then Twist, IK / FK Blend and Reverse Foot as needed.
Finish with APEX Configure Controls to set control shape, size and colour.

facts.text: Each AutoRig component adds one kind of rig function, chosen with its Component Source parameter; the docs chain one AutoRig node per function.
Multi IK Segments take tag names (for example *arm *leg), not #tag patterns.
Reverse Foot uses Segments, Ankle, Ball and IK Driven; IK Driven defaults to #ik_tip.
Bone Deform uses a Rest Skeleton, Rest Geo and Output Geo.

verify.text: After packing, the rig tree view shows the shape and skeleton folders.
The FK Transform component creates Base.rig in the character; pose the rig to test it.

mistakes.text: Writing #tag in the Multi IK Segments field: it expects the plain tag names.

phrases: attach the mesh to the skeleton in houdini
make the mesh follow the bones
bind the geometry to the joints
my fingers move with the wrong bone

ui.options_in: viewer state handle toggle, not a node parameter
shelf tool dialog, not a node

prerequisites: The skin geometry is polygonal and the skeleton is a SOP skeleton.
The skeleton is in a pose with the bones angled slightly, and the geometry curved slightly, so the capture knows which way each joint bends.

outline.text: Create capture weights with Joint Capture Biharmonic (organic shapes), or Joint Capture Proximity (simple shapes), giving it the skin geometry and the skeleton.
Connect Joint Deform after the capture node.
Pose with Rig Pose (display flag on Joint Deform, then Show Handle) and watch the deformation.

facts.text: Joint Capture Biharmonic gives smoothed weights from joint position and volume and suits soft organic deformation; Joint Capture Proximity is faster and distance-based; Capture Packed Geometry gives rigid 100% weights per piece; Joint Capture Paint paints weights by hand.
The weights are stored on the boneCapture attribute and are normalised per point.
The Capture Geometry shelf tool offers Type Biharmonic, Proximity or Regions; Max Iterations and High Precision only matter for Biharmonic.

verify.text: In Rig Pose, move a joint: the nearby skin follows it and does not tear.
Display the capture node to see joint regions, or read the boneCapture attribute in the geometry spreadsheet.

mistakes.text: Using NURBS shapes as capture shapes: only polygonal geometry works.
Clicking Reload Node Names on the Merge Packed node after assigning shapes: it reverts the shape names and breaks the assignments.
Leaving the bones perfectly straight: angle them slightly so the capture knows which way to bend.

symptom_phrases: fingers move with the wrong finger
weights bleed between fingers
eyelids move with the eye bone
mesh tears when one joint rotates
finger weights overlap in houdini
troubleshooting.cause: The default enlargement of the tet mesh used by the biharmonic capture makes close-together parts (fingers, eyelids) overlap, so neighbouring bones claim each other's points.
fix: Lower the enlargement of the tet embed (one user got to 0.2; it reduced but did not remove the overlap) or use tet conform.
Use proximity capture for the hands, or space the fingers further apart in the T-pose.
Leave eyes and face bones out of the first capture and weight them in a second pass.
For a hero character, paint the weights by hand.

symptom_phrases: jacket does not line up with the body
fbx character looks wrong in houdini
separate piece captured in a different rest pose
troubleshooting.cause: A piece (for example a jacket) was captured in a different rest pose from the body, and KineFX did not handle the mismatch in that thread.
fix: Adjust that piece's rest pose in Houdini so it matches the body.
Or fix the geometry in the source application and capture it again.
The thread ends without a confirmed fix; report it to SideFX with the file.

phrases: build the skeleton with the skeleton node
add joints to the character in houdini
make a joint chain in houdini

ui.options_in: viewer state toolbar, not node parameters

prerequisites: You are working at SOP level, in a geometry network, because the Skeleton node is a SOP.

outline.text: Add a Skeleton node and work in its viewport state. In Create mode click in empty space to make a joint; click a joint to create a new joint parented to it; Shift-click in empty space for a floating, unparented joint.
Press F to switch between Create and Modify mode. In Modify mode click a joint to select it, double-click to select its whole chain, hold S and drag to box select.
Press G for Tweak Mode and drag a joint to move it and its descendants; Shift-drag moves only that joint.
Give each joint a name in the Name field of the toolbar.

facts.text: Joint Placement offers View Based, Normal Based, Freehand and Surface. Freehand snaps to the construction plane if it is shown, otherwise the joint sits on a plane perpendicular to the view.
Delete removes the selected joint and reparents its descendants to its former parent; Shift+Delete removes it without reparenting them. Shift+Ctrl-click a link inserts a new joint into it.
Joints are white when unselected and yellow when selected; red joints mean the hierarchy contains a cycle.
The Skeleton node is a non-procedural, interactive way to author a skeleton; a skeleton is points connected by polygon lines.

verify.text: No joint is red: a red joint means a cyclical, invalid hierarchy that must be fixed.

mistakes.text: Using Stash Input when you want to keep your work: it removes all existing changes and copies the input. Use Stash Merge Input to append instead.
Expecting Delete to remove a joint's children: it reparents them to the deleted joint's parent; Shift+Delete leaves them with their old parent chain broken.

phrases: set the aim and up axis of the joints
prerequisites: A SOP skeleton is connected to the node's input.

outline.text: Connect the skeleton to Orient Joints, choose the Forward Vector (the axis that points to the children) and the Up Vector.
Add chain operations in order: set up the Root settings before Spine, and orient an arm before its hand so the hand can inherit the arm's up vector.

facts.text: Each joint's forward axis is oriented toward its children and its up axis toward a user-selected target; the node always outputs rigid transforms (scale 1 on all axes).
Chain operations are Do Nothing, Root Only, Spine, Plane, Multi Plane, World Up Vector and Rotation Offset; Preferred Plane keeps up vectors consistent with Plane and Multi Plane.
For a biped, the Biped Setup SOP generates biped_* groups that make it easier to select chains.

verify.text: Use the viewer state together with the parameter editor to see what each chain operation does to the joints' axes.

mistakes.text: Using Plane on a perfectly straight chain: no plane can be computed, so the node shows a warning and falls back to Spine.

phrases: mirror the joints to the other side
build one arm and mirror it
prerequisites: Half of the skeleton exists as a SOP skeleton on the node's input.

outline.text: Build one half of the skeleton with the Skeleton node, connect it to Skeleton Mirror, and choose Reflect Using Mirror Plane (Direction and Origin).
Use Find Tokens and Replace Tokens (for example a left prefix replaced by a right one) so the duplicated joints get new names.

facts.text: Mirroring Style By Rotation mirrors posing only in rotation and flips animated translations, and avoids negative scales; By Scale mirrors rotation and translation but leaves inversely scaled transforms.
With Update Existing Joints on, transforms on joints already on the mirrored side are updated; with it off, duplicate joints are created with the same name.

verify.text: Joint names are unique after mirroring: the page expects names to be unique, topology-independent identifiers.

mistakes.text: Turning Update Existing Joints off: clashing joint names can quickly be introduced and the page warns this can cause instability.
Using By Scale for a rig that goes to a game engine or another package: the inverse-scaled transforms can be problematic there.

phrases: make an ik leg in houdini
add an ik goal and a twist control
prerequisites: A SOP skeleton on the first input and a second skeleton (or points) with the goal and optional twist points on the second input.

outline.text: Connect the skeleton to the first input and the IK driver points to the second input.
Type the joint names for Root Name, Mid Name and Tip Name (for example shoulder, elbow, wrist), then the Goal Name and optionally the Twist Name.

facts.text: IK Chains creates and evaluates two-bone IK solvers on a SOP skeleton. The chain joints are called Root, Mid and Tip; the page does not use the words Start Joint, End Joint or Pole Vector.
If Twist Name is left blank, the solver uses the position of the Mid joint as the pole vector.
Blend mixes between the input pose and the IK result; Orient Tip orients the tip joint to the goal; Stretch lets the chain stretch to reach the goal.
The KineFX introduction lists IK Chains and Full Body IK among the pre-APEX rig behaviour nodes; rigs in Houdini 20 and later are built as APEX graphs.

verify.text: Move the goal point: the Tip joint follows it, and the Mid joint bends toward the twist point, or toward its own position when none is given.

mistakes.text: Enabling Enable Multithreading for one or two chains: it comes with an overhead and should only be used for many chains.

prerequisites: A SOP skeleton on the input.

outline.text: Place Rig Doctor after you change a skeleton's topology (adding, removing or reparenting joints), so later nodes can rely on a fixed topology and a name attribute.

facts.text: Rig Doctor checks for empty point names, duplicate names and names containing spaces, a failed traversal of the hierarchy, unsorted skeletons and missing transform attributes.
On Failure can be Warning (geometry passes through) or Error (interrupts cooking of the downstream network).
Re-Orient To Child uses the average position when a joint has several children; leaf joints use their parent's position as the reference.

verify.text: The node reports no warnings or errors for names or hierarchy.

mistakes.text: Leaving On Failure at Error while experimenting: a failure stops everything downstream from cooking.

phrases: how does rigging work in houdini
where do i start rigging in houdini

outline.text: Build the skeleton and prepare a guide skeleton (extra joints, tags and properties).
Create skin capture weights on the geometry.
Build the rig with APEX graphs, prebuilt rig components or the Autorig Builder.
Assemble the elements into a packed character folder structure, then animate in the animate state or with SOPs.

facts.text: KineFX is the SOP-level character toolset for rigging, animation and retargeting; APEX is the rigging engine underneath it.
Only data in a packed character folder structure can be displayed in the animate state; characters do not need to be packed for SOP-based animation.
Before Houdini 20, rig logic and evaluation were tied together (Rig Pose and Bone Deform); tutorials from that time show a different workflow from APEX.

phrases: add a bone to the armature
make a bone chain in blender

ui.path: Add > Single Bone (Shift-A in Edit Mode)

prerequisites: An armature object exists and is in Edit Mode: bones can be added to an armature in Edit Mode.

outline.text: In the 3D Viewport, in Edit Mode on the armature, choose Add > Single Bone (Shift-A) to add a bone, then adjust Name, Space, Align, Length and Deform in the redo panel.

facts.text: A new bone is one unit long, oriented toward the global Z axis, with its root at the 3D cursor, with no parent, and with Deform enabled.
Disable Deform for control bones that should not affect mesh deformation.

verify.text: The new bone appears in the Outliner under the armature and is listed in the bone's Name field.

mistakes.text: Leaving Deform on for control bones: they will then move the mesh.

phrases: copy the rotation of a bone
make one bone follow another bones rotation
prerequisites: The bone or object that should follow exists, and a target object or bone to copy from.

outline.text: Add a Copy Rotation constraint to the owner bone or object and set its Target (and Bone, if the target is an armature).

facts.text: The constraint forces an object or bone to match the rotation of a target, and as a side effect removes shearing.
Mix decides how the target's rotation is combined with the owner's original rotation: Replace, Add, Before Original, After Original, or the deprecated Offset (Legacy).
Axis chooses which axes are copied and Invert flips the sign on chosen axes; Influence sets how strongly the constraint affects the owner.

verify.text: Rotate the target: the owner follows on the axes you enabled.

mistakes.text: Relying on the old Offset checkbox behaviour: it does not work correctly with multiple axes and is deprecated; use a Mix mode instead.

phrases: switch the parent of a bone
make a bone act like a child of another
prerequisites: The child bone or object and the target parent exist.

outline.text: Add a Child Of constraint to the child and set its Target to the parent object or bone.

facts.text: The constraint transforms an object or bone as though it were a child of the target; unlike plain parenting its Influence can be animated, which allows switching between parents over time.
The same Influence can mix several Child Of constraints into a weighted average of parents; if those parents are bones the armature may be a better choice.
Location, Rotation and Scale choose which axes of the child are affected.

verify.text: Move the target: the child follows, and its transform is not displaced when the constraint is enabled.

mistakes.text: Ignoring a jump when the constraint is enabled: if the child's transform is correct with the constraint disabled but wrong with it enabled, click Set Inverse.

ui.options_in: button text on the panel (not an RNA name, so not checked against the install)

prerequisites: An armature with bones; Edit Mode or Pose Mode to move bones between collections.

outline.text: In the Bone Collections panel create a collection, select bones, and click Assign to put the selected bones in the active collection.
Use the Visible (eye) toggle to hide a collection in the 3D Viewport, and Solo to show only that collection.

facts.text: Bones can belong to several collections at once. Move to Bone Collection (M in Edit or Pose Mode) unassigns the selected bones from all other collections first.
Collections can be nested by dragging one name onto another, or with Add Child Collection from the right-click menu.
Remove Unused deletes collections that have neither bones nor children.

phrases: mirror the skeleton to the other side
build one leg and mirror it

ui.path: Rigging menu set (F3) > Skeleton > Mirror Joints > options
ui.options_in: the Mirror Joint Options window, not node attributes

prerequisites: The parent joint of the chain you want to mirror exists and is selected.

outline.text: Select the parent joint of the chain, then choose Skeleton > Mirror Joints and open its options.
Choose Mirror Across (the plane), optionally type the old name text in Search For and the new text in Replace With so the copies are renamed, then click Mirror.

facts.text: The Mirror Across options represent a plane whose origin is at the parent joint of the original chain.
Mirror duplicates and flips the chain and closes the window; Apply does the same and leaves the window open; Close discards the settings.

verify.text: A copy of the chain exists on the other side of the plane, with the names you asked for in Replace With.

mistakes.text: Making the other half with Edit > Duplicate at a Scale of -1: the page says to use Skeleton > Mirror Joint instead.

phrases: add a joint to the chain in maya
insert a joint into the skeleton
add an extra joint in the middle of the arm

ui.path: Rigging menu set (F3) > Skeleton > Insert Joints

prerequisites: A joint chain exists; the joint you click becomes the parent of the new joint.

outline.text: Choose Skeleton > Insert Joints, click the joint that should be the parent of the new joint, then drag to where the new joint should go.
Repeat for more joints, then press Enter to exit the Insert Joint Tool.

facts.text: Bones for inserted joints are oriented automatically along the axes of the bones already in the chain; the tool has no tool settings.
For a bound character the bind pose adjusts automatically when you insert joints and the skin history is retained.

verify.text: The new joint appears in the chain in the Outliner under the joint you clicked.

mistakes.text: Expecting an inserted joint to move the skin: it influences nothing until you add it with Skin > Edit Influence > Add Influence.

phrases: make the eye look at a target
point an object at another object

ui.path: Animation or Rigging menu set > Constrain > Aim > options
ui.options_in: the Aim Constraint Options window, not node attributes

prerequisites: The object to turn and the target to aim at both exist.

outline.text: Select the target(s), then the object to constrain, and choose Constrain > Aim.
Set Aim Vector (the local axis that points at the target, default local +X) and Up Vector (default local +Y), then choose a World Up Type.

facts.text: World Up Type choices are Scene Up, Object Up, Object Rotation Up, Vector (the default) and None; the World Up Vector defaults to (0, 1, 0), the positive Y axis.
Object Up and Object Rotation Up use a world up object, which is given with the -wuo flag of the aimConstraint MEL command.
Weight sets how strongly the targets influence the orientation, from 0 to 10, default 1.

verify.text: Move the target: the constrained object keeps its aim axis pointing at it without spinning around that axis.

mistakes.text: Pointing the Up Vector in the same direction as the Aim Vector, or setting World Up Type to None: the constrained object then depends on motion history and can flip.

phrases: copy the left weights to the right

ui.options_in: the Mirror Skin Weights Options window, not node attributes

prerequisites: The mesh is bound to a skeleton whose two halves are joints that correspond to each other.

outline.text: Select the skinned mesh, choose Skin > Mirror Skin Weights, set Mirror Across and Direction, set Surface Association and Influence Association, then apply.

facts.text: Surface Association is Closest point on surface (the default), Raycast or Closest component; Influence Association pairs joints by Closest joint (the default for the first pass), One to one, Label or None, in up to two passes.
Normalize scales each vertex's influences so they total 1.0 (for example 1.2 and 0.8 become 0.6 and 0.4).
Reflection is disabled in the Paint Skin Weights Tool, so Skin > Mirror Skin Weights is the way to mirror weights.

verify.text: Paint Skin Weights on the target side shows weights that mirror the source side.

mistakes.text: Using One to one when the two sides do not have identical skeleton hierarchies.
Leaving a second Influence Association pass on when one pass is enough: set the second to None.

phrases: reset the scale of the object
clear the object transform but keep the shape
prerequisites: The object (the mesh you will skin) is selected in Object Mode.

outline.text: Select the object and use Apply > Transforms (Location, Rotation, Scale or Rotation & Scale) so the transform values become neutral while the object stays where it is.

facts.text: Applying transforms resets Location, Rotation or Scale values while visually keeping the object in place: the origin moves to the global origin, rotation becomes zero and scale becomes 1.0, and the geometry is adjusted so it looks unchanged.

Applying transforms can affect how modifiers, constraints and parenting behave, because they often depend on an object's transform values; objects with children apply the transform to the children too.
Corrective Flip Normals flips normals when a negative scale is applied, which avoids inverted shading.

verify.text: The object's Location is 0, Rotation is 0 and Scale is 1 in the Object properties, and the mesh has not moved or changed size in the viewport.

mistakes.text: Applying transforms after constraints or a parent are set up, or on an object that is already skinned: constraints, modifiers and parenting depend on those values and can change.

phrases: set the rest pose in blender
make the current pose the rest pose
change the t pose of the armature

ui.path: Apply > Pose as Rest Pose (Pose Mode)
ui.options_in: menu labels in the Apply menu; the operator itself is named "Apply Pose as Rest Pose" in Blender 5.2.2

prerequisites: The armature is in Pose Mode and posed the way you want its new rest pose to be.

outline.text: In Pose Mode pose the bones, then choose Apply > Pose as Rest Pose (or Pose Selected as Rest Pose for only the selected bones).

facts.text: Pose as Rest Pose applies the current bone transforms to the armature in Edit Mode, so the armature's undeformed state changes to the current pose; meshes deformed by the armature are reset to their undeformed state relative to the new rest pose.
Pose Selected as Rest Pose does the same for the selected bones only; unselected bones keep their original rest pose transforms.

verify.text: Clear the pose transforms (Clear Transform > All): the armature stays in the new pose.

mistakes.text: Applying a rest pose casually: it permanently changes the armature structure and can require re-binding or adjusting skinning, constraints, drivers, animations and exported assets.

phrases: put the armature back to rest
prerequisites: The armature is in Pose Mode.

outline.text: In Pose Mode select the bones (or none, to affect all) and use Clear Transform > All, or Alt-G, Alt-R and Alt-S for location, rotation and scale separately.

facts.text: All resets location, rotation and scaling of the selected bones to their default values; Alt-G, Alt-R and Alt-S clear them individually.
Reset Unkeyed clears the transforms to their keyframe state; Only Selected chooses between the selected bones and all bones.
In Envelope visualization Alt-S does not clear scale but scales the Distance influence area of the selected bones.

verify.text: Each bone returns to its rest position: location and rotation 0, scale 1 in the bone's Transform panel.

phrases: rotate the bones to pose the character
move the arm by rotating bones
prerequisites: The armature exists; for the mesh to follow, it is skinned to the armature.

outline.text: Switch the armature to Pose Mode, select a bone and rotate it; each child bone follows its parent.

facts.text: Edit Mode edits the default rest position of an armature and Object Mode transforms whole objects, so bones are posed in Pose Mode.
In rest position each bone has neutral values (0 for position and rotation, 1 for scale); editing a bone in Pose Mode creates an offset from its rest position.
Bone colours: gray default, blue wireframe in Pose Mode, green with a constraint, yellow with an IK solver constraint.

verify.text: The skinned mesh deforms as the bone rotates.

mistakes.text: Trying to pose bones in Edit Mode: that changes the rest position instead of creating a pose.

phrases: rotate the joints to pose the rig

options: Bake Current Input Pose to Animation Channels
Bake Input Sequence into Animation Channels

prerequisites: A SOP skeleton or rig is connected to the node's input.

outline.text: Add a Rig Pose node after the skeleton and use its viewport state: select a joint and rotate it. Q selects the parent joint, A the first child, Z the next sibling.

To turn poses into animation channels use the Bake buttons on the node (Bake Current Input Pose to Animation Channels, or Bake Input Sequence into Animation Channels for a range of frames). These are the labels on the node in Houdini 22.0.466; what each bake does exactly was not checked.

facts.text: Mode decides how an edit is applied: Pre-Multiply (the default) layers transforms on the input, typically for FK rotations; Post-Multiply changes the offset from the parent; Override replaces input animation; From Rest Pose restores a point to the pose in the Rest Pose Attribute.
Set All Transformations to Default returns Translate, Rotate and Scale to defaults even if animated; on an existing keyframe it replaces the animated values with defaults.
With joint limits from the Configure Joints SOP, Enforce Transform Limits (toggle with F) stops rotation past the limits.

verify.text: Moving a joint in the viewport changes the Transformations entries on the node and the joints below it follow.

mistakes.text: Changing World Space after you already have edits on the pose: it will likely produce erratic results; use separate Rig Pose nodes for mixed local and world-space edits.
Using Override and expecting input animation to survive: it replaces the input animation for that point.

phrases: save the current pose on the skeleton
prerequisites: A SOP skeleton in the pose you want to store.

outline.text: Connect the posed skeleton to Rig Stash Pose, name the point attribute in Attribute Name, set Mode to Store; later set Mode to Restore to apply it again.

facts.text: The node stores a static pose on a skeleton as a matrix point attribute for use downstream; with a second input connected, that input's pose is written to the attribute.
The documentation calls it a static pose; it does not call it a rest pose or bind pose, so whether you use it as a rest pose is your choice of workflow.

verify.text: After Restore, the skeleton returns to the stored pose.

mistakes.text: Choosing the Stash SOP method without knowing it is destructive: it replaces the current pose on the first input.
Leaving Clear Existing Attribute on by accident: it clears the existing point attribute before storing.

phrases: go to bind pose in maya
return the skeleton to the bind pose
reset the character to the t pose
snap the rig back to bind pose
skeleton wont go to bind pose

ui.path: Rigging menu set (F3) > Skin > Go To Bind Pose

prerequisites: The character's skeleton is bound to a surface (a bind pose exists).

outline.text: With one bind pose, select the character's skeleton and choose Skin > Go To Bind Pose; with several bound surfaces, select the surface you want returned to its bind pose first.

facts.text: When the skeleton will not reach its bind pose the cause is locked joint attributes (constraints, expressions, IK spline handles, IK handles with keys) or locked attributes or an expression on the root joint, whose pose is relative to world space.

verify.text: The joints return to the pose they had when the mesh was bound.

mistakes.text: Forgetting to turn the nodes back on after the fix: Modify > Evaluate Nodes > Ignore All must be followed by Evaluate All.

symptom_phrases: skeleton does not go to the bind pose
error can only reach local bind pose
go to bind pose fails
root joint did not reach bind pose
troubleshooting.cause: Joint attributes are locked by constraints, expressions, IK spline handles or IK handles with keys, or the root joint has locked attributes or an expression, so the skeleton cannot reach its bind pose.
fix: Choose Modify > Evaluate Nodes > Ignore All to disable the nodes that lock the attributes.
Choose Skin > Go To Bind Pose.
Choose Modify > Evaluate Nodes > Evaluate All to turn the nodes back on.
If the local-only bind pose error remains, check the root joint for locked attributes or expressions and repeat the three steps.

phrases: return the object to its original zero position

ui.options_in: the Reset Transformations options window, not node attributes

prerequisites: The object or control is selected.

outline.text: Select the object and choose Modify > Reset Transformations; open its options to leave Translate, Rotate or Scale out of the reset.

facts.text: Maya stores an object's transform as an offset from its original zero position. Reset Transformations returns the object to that zero (the first or last frozen position); Freeze Transformations makes the current transformations the new zero.

verify.text: The Channel Box shows 0 for translate and rotate and 1 for scale on the object.

mistakes.text: Expecting Reset Transformations to undo a freeze: it returns to the last or first frozen position, so the frozen reference matters.
